system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2178-02-11 21:43:00 to 2178-02-16 13:55:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis, insulin-dependent diabetes, morbid obesity, and recent MSSA cellulitis was admitted for bilateral neck swelling and facial edema causing shortness of breath. Initially admitted to the ICU for airway monitoring, he received IV dexamethasone and racemic epinephrine after developing respiratory distress during imaging. CT showed symmetrically enlarged parotid glands without abscess, consistent with sialadenitis. He was treated with IV clindamycin for possible bacterial superinfection, later discontinued as ENT and infectious disease concluded the inflammation was likely viral or related to his underlying psoriatic arthritis. A new pustular psoriasis rash on the chest and arms, triggered by steroid use, was managed with clobetasol. A fungal infection (tinea corporis) on the forearm was identified and treated with miconazole. His warfarin was held due to an INR of 4.8, then restarted and titrated to 4 mg daily with a therapeutic INR of 2.7 at discharge. He improved clinically, was weaned off IV therapy, and discharged home with outpatient follow-up and lab monitoring.
problems: Ulcer of other part of lower limb
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ year-old gentleman with a PMH of PE on 
warfarin, DM, psoriatic arthritis on chronic steroid therapy c/b 
secondary adrenal insufficiency, now presenting with dizziness, 
chest pain, episode of syncope

# Syncope- Unclear etiology. Patient reportedly orthostatic at 
home, borderline orthostatic (and symptomatic with standing) 
throughout hospitalization. Initial differential included 
adrenal insufficiency, but no improvement with increased dose of 
steroids and electrolytes normal. Per endocrinology consult, 
home dose of steroids is supraphysiologic, so adrenal 
insufficiency unlikely to be culprit from their perspective. 
Possible that mineralocorticoid deficiency secondary to 
spironolactone contributing, but no change in symptoms with 
holding that medication. Less likely volume depletion, as no 
improvement with 500cc bolus and holding furosemide, 
spironolactone and HCTZ. Furosemide restarted prior to 
discharge, HCTZ and spironolactone held. Cardiac etiology also 
high on ddx given exertional chest tightness and dyspnea on 
exertion, as well as risk factors for CAD(DM, obesity, htn), 
however troponins negative, echo not significantly changed from 
previous (both poor quality) and nuclear stress test normal. 
Frequent ectopy on telemetry, but no sustained events or 
correlation with symptoms. Postulated that enlarged parotids and 
facial/neck tissues could be causing compression of carotid 
baroreceptors, leading to syncope, although unclear whether this 
is possible. Patient scheduled for outpatient ENT follow-up.

# Sialoadenitis- The patient presents with a massive 
sialoadenitis involving the parotid glands and submandibular 
glands. The etiology has not been defined. The patient has 
positive mumps IgG but negative IgM, antibiotics did not 
modified the size of the enlargement suggesting that a bacterial 
infection was not responsible. Multiple subspeciality workups 
have been undertaken without etiology discovered. Touched base 
with ENT, who said that based on their prior evaluation and 
review of the imaging, this is consistent with fatty infiltrate 
and there is no indication for biopsy at this time. Repeat CT 
neck unchanged from prior. Patient scheduled for outpatient ENT 
evaluation. 
 
#HTN- continued carvediolol, lisinopril with reasonable BP 
control. Diuretics held as above. continued baby aspirin and 
atorvastatin

# History of PE: INR subtherapeutic on admission. Bridged with 
Lovenox, increased warfarin dose to 7.5mg daily.

# Psoriatic Arthritis- pt has been tried on many different 
immunosuppressive therapies by rheum and the pt has either 
failed them or treatment has been complicated by infection. 
Currently pt is only on dexamethasone, tenative plans to start 
cyclosporine in the future. 

# Elevated LDH: unclear etiology. Quite elevated (700s on day of 
discharge), out of proportion to mild liver enzyme elevation, no 
evidence cardiac ischemia. No lymphadenopathy in cervical or 
mediastinal regions (or on CT of abdomen/pelvis in ___. 
Previously elevated in ___, but not to the same degree. No 
evidence of hemolysis. Germ cell tumors are also on the 
differential for very high LDH, so AFP sent and pending at time 
of discharge.

# LLE wound- infected with MSSA in past, now off antibiotics and 
it is healing well currently. On exam dressing is clean, dry and 
intact, no purulent drainage from wound. No evidence of 
infection. Daily dressing changes per wound care.   

# Adrenal Insufficiency- pt is adrenally insufficient after 
prolonged courses of steroids in the past. Now requiring daily 
dexamethasone replacement. Taper has been attempted in the past, 
but complicated by psoriatic arthritis flares and frequent 
admissions for other issues. Continue bactrim prophylaxis.
  
# Chronic pain- followed by pain service. Continued tizanidine, 
nortryptiline and PO dilaudid at home doses.

# Nosebleeds: patient complained of multiple nosebleeds ___, 
all of which stopped spontaneously with pressure. He was not 
hemodynamically unstable, and had no change in his hematocrit.

# diagnosis of adjustment disorder with anxious features by 
psychiatry in ___. psychiatry evaluation prompted by 
concerns that patient was harming himself or tampering with 
medical care (injecting substances into ___, shaking telemetry 
box to mimic vtach, not taking medications such as warfarin as 
directed). See discharge summaries from ___ for further 
details. No major issues during this hospitalization.
 
# DM- continued basal and short acting insulin regimen  
# HEALTH CARE ___ ___  
# CODE STATUS: full

therapeutic
- check chemistry panel ___ to monitor potassium. 
Patient did not need potassium supplementation during 
hospitalization, however, was only recently re-started on

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___? I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. I've been reviewing your case. You came in after passing out, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. I felt dizzy getting off the plane, then just blacked out. I’ve been feeling faint for days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your wife mentioned your blood pressure drops when you stand. We call that orthostatic hypotension. We’ll look into why that’s happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been holding my blood pressure meds—lisinopril, carvedilol, and the diuretics—because I thought they were making me dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll check your labs and monitor your vitals. We also need to rule out serious causes like a heart issue or pulmonary embolism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a pulmonary embolism before. I’m on warfarin. Is that still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was 1.9 on arrival—just below therapeutic. We’ve bridged you with Lovenox and increased your warfarin to 7.5 mg daily to get it back in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also had this chest tightness and shortness of breath when I walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. Your EKG showed sinus tachycardia and some extra beats, but no signs of a heart attack. Troponin was negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t rule it out completely, but your stress test and echo will help. Given your diabetes and weight, heart disease is a concern, but so far, no clear evidence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my neck? It’s been swollen and tender for weeks. Feels worse now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. Your parotid and submandibular glands are enlarged. We did a CT of your neck and chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected again? I had sialadenitis before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows no abscess or inflammation. The glands are fatty-replaced and symmetrically enlarged—unchanged from your last scan. No signs of bacterial infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it? Cancer? Something serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of cancer. ENT reviewed the images and thinks it’s likely fatty infiltration, possibly related to your long-term steroid use. No biopsy needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steroids? I’ve been on dexamethasone for years for my arthritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s also why you have adrenal insufficiency. Your body doesn’t make its own cortisol anymore. We’ll keep you on your 4.5 mg daily dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had nosebleeds too. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They stopped on their own, and your blood count is stable. Likely from dry air or irritation. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your white count is a bit high, and your LDH is very elevated—897.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: LDH? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a marker of cell turnover. Could be from muscle, liver, heart, or even tumors. But your liver enzymes are only mildly up, and no heart damage. No lymph nodes on imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what could it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure. Could be related to your chronic inflammation or steroid use. We’ve sent an AFP to check for rare causes like germ cell tumors. It’s pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dizziness? Any answers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you a fluid bolus, but no improvement. Endocrinology says your steroid dose is already high, so adrenal crisis is unlikely. We’re holding your diuretics for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do a nuclear stress test today to check your heart. And we’ll repeat the LDH and INR tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stress test came back normal. No signs of ischemia. Your heart function is likely okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I still feel faint when I stand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering if your enlarged neck tissues are pressing on the carotid sinus, which could cause fainting. ENT will see you as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds strange. Is that possible?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s rare, but possible. We’ll refer you for a tilt table test and neurology consult after discharge to explore that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the neck CT results. Still shows the same fatty parotid enlargement. No new lesions or inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s stable. We’re not treating it as an infection since antibiotics didn’t help before. We’ll follow up with ENT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show LDH is still high—720—but trending down. INR is now 2.7, which is perfect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the warfarin is working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll keep you on 7.5 mg daily. We’re restarting furosemide, but holding HCTZ and spironolactone for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why stop those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They might be contributing to your dizziness. We’ll see how you do without them and adjust based on your weight and swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My leg wound—is it healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the dressing is clean, no signs of infection. You’re off antibiotics, and wound care will continue at the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your condition is stable, and we’ve ruled out major issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where am I going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To an extended care facility for a few days. They’ll help with mobility, monitor your blood pressure, and manage your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see ENT for your neck, cardiology for the stress test results, and your rheumatologist. We’re also checking AFP and scheduling a tilt table test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my steroids? Should I keep taking them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue the dexamethasone. Endocrinology and rheumatology are discussing starting cyclosporine to possibly reduce your steroid dose long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stop HCTZ and spironolactone for now. Warfarin is now 7.5 mg daily. Keep all your other medications the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nosebleeds or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Report any severe nosebleeds. For dizziness, check your weight daily and avoid sudden standing. The outpatient workup will help clarify things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel better just knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up closely. We’re here if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis, secondary adrenal insufficiency, morbid obesity, and prior pulmonary embolism was admitted for syncope and dizziness. He had been experiencing orthostatic symptoms and an episode of fainting after standing, prompting evaluation for cardiac, metabolic, and neurologic causes. Workup revealed a subtherapeutic INR, which was corrected with warfarin dose adjustment and bridging anticoagulation. Cardiac testing, including a nuclear stress test and echocardiogram, showed no evidence of ischemia or significant dysfunction, though image quality was limited by body habitus. His chronic bilateral parotid and submandibular gland enlargement, consistent with fatty infiltration and sialadenitis, remained stable on imaging with no signs of infection or malignancy. LDH was markedly elevated without clear etiology, prompting further outpatient evaluation. Diuretics were held due to persistent dizziness, with furosemide restarted before discharge while spironolactone and HCTZ were discontinued. He was discharged to extended care with plans for outpatient ENT, neurology, and cardiology follow-up, along with monitoring of INR, electrolytes, and pending AFP results.
